title: Expositio Psalmi CXVIII
author: Ambrose

passages.original: unde puto et Pythagoram illum philosophum imitatorem iuuenis huius prophetici instituisse sectam, ut discipuli sui quinquennio non loquentes tanto silentio loqui discerent, cum praesertim et Dauid superioris aetatis quam Pythagoram fuisse non dubium sit, qui ait: dixi: custodiam uias meas, ut non delinquam in lingua mea; posui ori meo custodiam. et quia forte aliquando aliquid
passages.english: Hence I think that Pythagoras too, that well-known philosopher, as an imitator of this prophetic young man, established his school so that his disciples, not speaking for five years, might learn to speak by so long a silence; especially since there is no doubt that David too was of an earlier age than Pythagoras, he who says: "I said: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue; I have set a guard on my mouth." And because perhaps at some time something
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-sentence ("et quia forte aliquando aliquid"); the continuation is not given. The psalm quoted is Ps. 38(39):2. "Tanto silentio" literally means "by so great a silence"; it is rendered "by so long a silence".

passages.original: etenim quasi fabulae cuiusdam naenias narratas sibi dicit ἀδολεσχίας, hoc est superfluas loquacitates. narratores enim superflui sicut hirundines disputationis suauitatem natiuae loquacitatis continuatione corrumpunt, ut Aristotelis sententia est.
passages.english: For he says that what were told to him were, as it were, the idle tales of some story, *adoleschiai*, that is, superfluous chatter. For superfluous storytellers, like swallows, spoil the sweetness of a discussion by the unbroken continuance of their native talkativeness, as is the opinion of Aristotle.
passages.notes: Greek ἀδολεσχίας ("idle talk, garrulity") is kept in transliteration because Ambrose glosses it himself. "Naenias" (nenias), literally "dirges", is used here in the sense "trifles, idle tales". The comparison of chatterers with swallows is attributed to Aristotle; the source was not identified.
